introduction-the-swiss-army-knife-proble.core: General-purpose operating systems include drivers, services, shells and syscalls for every possible workload, but a single cloud service uses a tiny fraction. That extra code costs boot time, memory and attack surface. Unikernels ask: what if each application shipped with only the OS parts it needs?

first_principles.problem: A microservice VM boots a full Linux with hundreds of unused components just to run one HTTP server.
truths: Unused code still runs or loads.
derivation: **Link** needed OS functions into the app.

analogy.title: Carrying a full Swiss Army knife to open one bottle
analogy.story: A simple bottle opener would be lighter and quicker.
analogy.breaks: Knives don't get hacked; unused OS code can be exploited.

example.title: What a web service uses
flow: Needs: network stack, memory allocator, timers, maybe a filesystem
Doesn't need: USB, shells, users, cron, dozens of daemons

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Most of the OS is dead weight for one app.

check.a: General-purpose OSes ship far more functionality than a single application needs, adding cost and attack surface.

the-concept-libraryos.core: A library operating system implements OS services (network stack, filesystem, scheduler, memory management) as libraries that link directly into the application, instead of a separate kernel accessed through syscalls. Calls become ordinary function calls in one address space, removing context switches.

first_principles.problem: Syscalls and kernel/user transitions add overhead to every I/O operation.
truths: OS functions can be implemented as libraries.

analogy.title: A chef who keeps all needed tools at their own station
analogy.story: No walking to a shared tool room for every task.
analogy.breaks: Chefs can still share a kitchen; library OSes usually run one app per VM.

example.title: Calling the network stack
flow: Linux: app → syscall → kernel TCP stack → driver
LibOS: app → tcp_send() library call → driver
example.outcome: OS services without a kernel boundary.

check.q: How does a library OS avoid syscall overhead?
check.a: OS services are linked into the application and invoked as normal function calls in one address space.

what-is-a-unikernel.core: A unikernel is a single-address-space machine image built by compiling an application together with just the library-OS components it needs, booting directly on a hypervisor (or bare metal). There's one process, no shell, no users and often no ability to run other programs, so the image is tiny and specialised.

first_principles.problem: People can't picture how an app can run without a traditional OS underneath.
truths: An app plus drivers can boot directly.
Single-purpose systems need no multi-user features.

analogy.title: A single-purpose appliance like a toaster
analogy.story: It boots instantly, does one job well and has no settings menu to break.
analogy.breaks: Toasters can't be patched; unikernels are rebuilt and redeployed for updates.

example.title: Image size
flow: Ubuntu VM with nginx: ~1 GB image

check.q: What runs inside a unikernel besides the application?
check.a: Only the library-OS components the application needs, in a single address space.

unikernels-vs-containers-vs-vms.core: VMs give strong isolation (own kernel) but are heavy. Containers are light but share the host kernel. Unikernels combine VM-level isolation (hypervisor boundary) with container-like size and boot speed, at the cost of specialisation: limited language/runtime support, difficult debugging and rebuilds for changes.

first_principles.problem: A team needs strong isolation and fast boot and can't decide between VMs, containers and unikernels.
truths: Isolation strength depends on the boundary.
Size and boot depend on what's included.

analogy.title: Detached houses, shared flats and custom tiny homes
analogy.story: Houses are separate but big; flats share walls; tiny homes are separate and small but suit only minimalists.
analogy.breaks: Tiny homes can be lived in by anyone patient; unikernels need apps that fit their constraints.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Specialisation pays only in specific niches.

check.q: What isolation boundary does a unikernel use?
check.a: The hypervisor (each unikernel is its own VM).

the-benefits-speed-size-and-efficiency.core: Unikernels boot in milliseconds, images are kilobytes to a few megabytes, memory footprints are small, and specialisation can raise network throughput by skipping kernel/user transitions. With fewer components there's less attack surface: no shell to pop, no unused services and often an immutable image.

first_principles.problem: Scale-to-zero services suffer cold starts, and VM sprawl wastes memory.

analogy.title: A racing bicycle stripped of extras
analogy.story: Lighter, faster and fewer parts to break, but no cargo rack.
analogy.breaks: Bikes don't get hacked; security benefits depend on the remaining code's quality.

example.title: Scale-to-zero function
flow: Requests served on demand without idle capacity

check.q: Why do unikernels have a smaller attack surface?
check.a: They include only the code the app needs, with no shell, unused services or general-purpose interfaces.

the-ecosystem-mirageos-and-unikraft.core: MirageOS is a clean-slate unikernel framework in OCaml, with type-safe, modular libraries, used for network appliances and secure services. Unikraft is a modular, POSIX-compatible unikernel kit that runs many existing apps (nginx, Redis, Python, Node) with configuration via Kraftfile and kraft CLI. Others include OSv, Nanos and HermitCore.

first_principles.problem: Teams want unikernel benefits without rewriting their apps in a niche language.
derivation: **Unikraft** for POSIX apps with minimal changes.

analogy.title: Two custom-bike builders
analogy.story: One builds from scratch in a special material; the other adapts standard parts to fit lighter frames.
analogy.breaks: Bike builders serve hobbyists; unikernel projects need production tooling and support.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: nginx as a few-MB unikernel VM.

check.q: Which unikernel project focuses on running existing POSIX applications?

unikernels-in-practice-where-they-fit.core: Unikernels fit niches: network functions and appliances (firewalls, DNS, proxies), high-density or scale-to-zero serverless, security-critical single services, edge and IoT with tight resources, and research. They're less suitable where you need rich debugging, many dependencies, dynamic workloads or a mature operations ecosystem.

first_principles.problem: A team considers rewriting all microservices as unikernels.
truths: Operational tooling matters for most teams.
Not every benefit is needed everywhere.
derivation: Choose **narrow, stable, performance- or security-critical** services.

analogy.title: Racing cars on a track versus delivery vans
analogy.story: Racing cars win on the track; vans do daily deliveries better.
analogy.breaks: Racing cars can't be driven on roads; unikernels can serve production, but only in fitting roles.

example.title: Good candidate
flow: Unikernel image 3 MB, boots in 10 ms

check.q: Name a workload well suited to unikernels.
check.a: A network function such as a DNS server, proxy or firewall (also scale-to-zero serverless).
